lead: An interaction diagram draws one scenario from a use case: which objects take part, what messages they send each other, and in what order. Two forms are covered here: the sequence diagram and the collaboration diagram, called the communication diagram in UML 2. UML 2 also has timing and interaction overview diagrams. The sequence diagram puts time down the page, so you read the story top to bottom. The collaboration diagram puts the same story on a web of links and carries the order in nested numbers. Teams use these diagrams to check a design against its use cases before any code is written.
prereq: You need 3.6 for the objects and the classes they come from, and Unit 2, Scenario-based modeling and use cases, for the scenarios themselves.

blocks.text: A use case says what the system does for an actor. A scenario is one path through that use case — the happy path, or one failure path. An interaction diagram draws one scenario as objects and the messages they exchange. It answers a question a class diagram cannot: at run time, who talks to whom, and in what order.

Three words carry the whole chapter. An object is one instance of a class from 3.6, written as name:Class with the whole name underlined, or as :Class when the name is not needed. A message is a request one object sends to another; it has a name, arguments and a direction. A link is a connection between two objects along which messages can travel. Links come from the associations in the class diagram.

One diagram shows one scenario, not every path. A use case with five scenarios gets five interaction diagrams, or one diagram with frames that select between the paths. Drawing everything at once gives a picture nobody can read.

sections.h3: Sequence diagram: time runs down the page

blocks.text: Each actor or object sits in a box across the top, with a dashed vertical line, the lifeline, hanging below it. Time runs downward, so a message drawn lower happens later. The left-to-right order of the boxes is free; the usual habit is actor on the left, the objects it drives to the right.

A message is an arrow from one lifeline to another, labelled with its name and arguments. The narrow rectangle on a lifeline is an activation bar: the object is busy handling a call while the bar is drawn. Bars nest, because a call made inside a call keeps the caller active.

head: Arrow
Meaning
rows: Synchronous call; the sender waits for the return
Asynchronous call; the sender carries on without waiting
Return, the reply to an earlier call

blocks.text: Objects can appear and disappear. A «create» message points at a box placed lower down, because that object did not exist earlier. A small X at the end of a lifeline marks destruction.

Frames group messages. A frame is a rectangle with a pentagon label in the corner. The alt frame has two or more operands separated by a dashed line, each carrying a guard in square brackets, and exactly one operand runs. The loop frame repeats its contents; write the count or the condition in the label, as in loop(3) or loop[while more items].

sections.h3: Collaboration diagram: numbering carries the order

blocks.text: A collaboration diagram draws the same objects as boxes joined by links. There is no time axis and no lifeline. Messages sit on or beside a link as small arrows, each labelled with a number that fixes its order.

The numbering is nested. The first message of the scenario is 1. A message sent while handling message 1 is 1.1; a message sent while handling 1.1 is 1.1.1. When message 1 is fully handled, the next top-level message is 2, and its sub-messages are 2.1, 2.2 and so on. The depth of the number is the depth of the call, and reading the numbers in order reproduces the top-to-bottom order of the sequence diagram.

items: List the objects that take part and draw one box for each; link the pairs that exchange messages.
Walk the sequence diagram from top to bottom. Give each new top-level message the next whole number 1, 2, 3 …
When a message is sent while another is being handled, add a decimal level to the current number: 1.1, then 1.1.1, and so on.

blocks.text: To convert back, read the numbers in ascending order and draw each message as a new arrow, top to bottom.

A return is drawn dashed and is not a new call. Because the layout is free, a collaboration diagram stays compact when there are many objects; a sequence diagram is easier to follow when the story is long and full of returns.

figure.caption: The same ATM scenario in both views. The sequence diagram puts time down the page, 4 calls and 3 dashed returns; the collaboration diagram puts the same 7 messages on 2 links and keeps the order in the numbers 1, 1.1, 2, 2.1.

spec.aria: Left: a sequence diagram with lifelines User, ATM and Bank and seven arrows from insert card down to cash, returns dashed. Right: a collaboration diagram with User linked to ATM and ATM linked to Bank, the messages numbered 1, 1.1, 2 and 2.1.

examples.question: Convert this sequence into a collaboration diagram: the user inserts a card (call 1), the ATM asks the bank to verify the PIN (call 1.1), the bank replies OK (return on 1.1), the user asks for ₹2,000 (call 2), the ATM debits the bank (call 2.1), the bank approves (return on 2.1), the ATM hands out the cash (return on 2). (a) Write the numbering. (b) How many links are there, and how many messages travel on each?
steps: Objects: User (an actor), ATM and Bank. Draw three boxes.
Links: messages travel between User and ATM, and between ATM and Bank. No message goes directly from User to Bank, so there is no User–Bank link. That is 2 links.
Number the first top-level call: 'insert card' is 1. Sent while handling it, 'verify PIN' is 1.1. The PIN reply is a return; draw it dashed and label it with the call it answers, 1.1.

The first call is fully handled, so the next top-level call, 'withdraw ₹2,000', is 2. Inside it, 'debit ₹2,000' is 2.1. The approval is a return on 2.1, and the cash is a return on 2. Draw both dashed.
Count messages per link. User–ATM: call 1, call 2 and the cash return on 2, that is 3 messages. ATM–Bank: call 1.1, its return, call 2.1 and its return, that is 4 messages.
Check: 3 + 4 = 7 messages, the same seven arrows as the sequence diagram.
examples.answer: The calls are numbered 1, 1.1, 2, 2.1. The returns are dashed and carry the number of the call they answer: PIN reply on 1.1, approval on 2.1, cash on 2. There are 2 links: User–ATM carries 3 messages and ATM–Bank carries 4 messages.
examples.check:
count = {}
for m in ['User-ATM', 'ATM-Bank', 'Bank-ATM', 'User-ATM', 'ATM-Bank', 'Bank-ATM', 'ATM-User']:
    a, b = m.split('-')
    key = '-'.join(sorted([a, b]))
    count[key] = count.get(key, 0) + 1
print(len(count))
print(count['ATM-User'])
print(count['ATM-Bank'])

traps: Writing message numbers on a sequence diagram, or drawing a time axis on a collaboration diagram. Sequence means time down the page and no numbers; collaboration means numbers on links and no time axis.
Treating a return as a new call. A return is a dashed arrow with an open arrowhead. A return closes the callee's activation bar. It never opens a new activation bar.
Drawing every scenario of a use case on one diagram. One interaction diagram holds one scenario; the rest need their own diagram or an alt frame.
Mixing up alt and loop. alt picks exactly one operand out of several; loop repeats the same operand.
Forgetting the guard condition in square brackets on alt operands, so the reader cannot tell when each branch runs.

quiz.q: What is a lifeline in a sequence diagram?
quiz.a: The dashed vertical line below an actor or object box. It shows the object exists over time, and messages arrive at and leave from points along it.

quiz.q: Which arrow shows a synchronous message, and which shows a return?
quiz.a: Synchronous: a solid line with a filled arrowhead. Return: a dashed line with an open arrowhead.

quiz.q: Why does a collaboration diagram not need a time axis?
quiz.a: Because the nested numbering 1, 1.1, 1.1.1, 2 … fixes the order. The reader follows the numbers, so the boxes can be laid out however is clearest.

quiz.q: A sequence shows: the user logs in (first message); inside that call the system checks the database; the database replies; then the user opens a report; inside that call the system fetches data from the database; the database replies. Write the nested numbers for a collaboration diagram.
quiz.a: Calls: 1 login, 1.1 check, 2 open report, 2.1 fetch data. The two database replies are returns, drawn dashed and labelled with the call they answer: reply on 1.1 and reply on 2.1. Depth follows calls only; the database check sits inside login and the fetch sits inside open report.

quiz.q: Messages in a collaboration diagram: call 1 (A→B), call 1.1 (B→C), return on 1.1 (C→B), call 2 (B→A), call 2.1 (B→C). How many links are there, and how many messages travel on each?
quiz.a: Two links. A–B carries calls 1 and 2, that is 2 messages. B–C carries call 1.1, its return, and call 2.1, that is 3 messages. Total 5 messages.

quiz.q: A student numbers the arrows 1 to 7 down the left side of a sequence diagram. What is wrong, and what should replace the numbers?
quiz.a: The ordering is already carried by vertical position, so the numbers are redundant and non-standard. Remove them. Nothing replaces them: vertical position alone shows the order; if order must be made explicit, nested numbers go on the collaboration diagram instead.

quiz.q: During a withdrawal the ATM either dispenses cash or shows 'insufficient funds'. Which combined fragment do you use, and what goes in the brackets? Why is loop wrong here?
quiz.a: alt, with two operands. Guards: [balance ≥ amount] on the first, [else] on the second. loop is wrong because only one branch runs once, not a repetition.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry these diagrams are usually generated from text: PlantUML and Mermaid turn a few lines into a sequence diagram, and UML tools can rebuild one from a running trace. Telecom standards use message sequence charts, the same idea with a formal semantics, and model checkers can prove that a set of scenarios never leaves a message unanswered. Each scenario also becomes a test case during integration testing — see Unit 4. Useful search terms: 'sequence diagram alt fragment', 'PlantUML sequence', 'message sequence chart'.
